title: Preventing Kitchen Accidents
bigQuestion: What do you do in the first ten seconds of a kitchen emergency, and how do you keep it from happening at all?

story.title: The Pan That Caught Fire
story.kicker: It was the third week of cooking lab, the oil was too hot, and somebody reached for a cup of water.
paragraphs: Station four was frying plantains. Jayden had the skillet on high with a quarter inch of oil in it, and he turned around to find the spatula. When he turned back, the oil was smoking, then it was not smoke anymore. Flames rose off the surface of the oil in a low, orange sheet. Somebody screamed. Somebody else laughed, then stopped laughing.

Lena at the next station grabbed a measuring cup, filled it at the sink and started toward the stove. Ms. Okafor's voice cut through the room. "No water. Lena, put it down." Lena froze with the cup in her hand. Water on burning oil does not put it out. It flashes to steam under the oil and throws the burning grease into the air.

Ms. Okafor was already at the stove. She reached past the pan, not over it, and turned the burner off. Then she took the skillet's lid from the hook on the wall, held it like a shield with the oven mitt, and slid it over the pan from the near edge. The flames went out under the lid the moment the air was gone. She left the lid on and the pan where it was.

"Nobody touches that pan for twenty minutes," she said. "If you lift the lid now, the air goes back in and it can light again." She pointed at the red extinguisher by the door. "That was next, if the lid had not worked. And 911 after that, from the hallway, not from in here."

Jayden was shaking. Nothing was burned but a little oil and his pride. That afternoon the class did not cook. They walked through what had happened, second by second: the oil left on high, the turn away from the stove, the water, the lid. By the end of the period every student could say the three things you do for a grease fire, in order, without looking at the board.
story.think: Ms. Okafor did three things in order: burner off, lid on, leave it alone. What would have gone wrong if she had skipped any one of them?

lessons.title: Burns and Scalds
lessons.mainIdea: Most kitchen burns come from steam, hot handles and splashing oil, and every one of them is preventable.
reading: Lift the lid off a pot of boiling pasta and tilt it toward you. The steam that rolls out is over 212 °F and it burns skin instantly. That is a *scald*, a burn from hot liquid or steam, and it is the most common kitchen injury. Always lift a lid away from your face, so the steam escapes on the far side. Open the oven door partway and wait a second before leaning in.

Handles are the next problem. A pot handle sticking out over the front of the stove is a handle someone will hit with an elbow. Turn every handle toward the back or the side, over the counter, not over another burner. A metal handle on a skillet that has been in the oven is as hot as the oven. Leave the mitt on it, or drape a towel over it, so the next person knows.

Use dry *oven mitts* or pot holders, never a wet towel; water in the cloth turns to steam against your hand. Set hot pans on a trivet or a cooling rack, not on the counter or on a plastic cutting board. Pull the oven rack out to reach a dish instead of reaching into the oven. When you add food to hot oil, lower it in with tongs so it does not splash.

Microwaves cause their own burns. A bowl can be cool while the food inside is far hotter, and liquids heated too long can boil up suddenly when moved. Let food stand a minute, stir it, and take it out with a mitt. Keep small children away from the stove entirely, and keep the cords of kettles and slow cookers pushed back where nobody can pull them.

words.d: a burn caused by hot liquid or steam
a thick, dry glove for holding hot pans; a wet one turns to steam and burns
a heatproof stand that a hot pot rests on so it does not burn the counter

look.title: Spot the Burn Waiting to Happen
look.text: A stove with four burners. Front left: a pot of boiling water with the handle pointing straight out into the room. Back right: a skillet that just came out of a 425 °F oven, sitting with its bare metal handle facing forward. A damp dish towel hangs over the oven door. A student is about to lift the pasta pot's lid straight up toward her face.
look.prompt: Name every burn hazard in this scene and say what you would change about each one.

check.q: How should you lift the lid off a boiling pot?
choices: Tilted away from your face so the steam goes the other way
Tilted toward you so you can see inside
With a wet towel for grip
check.why: Steam escapes on the side the lid opens; tilting it away keeps the scald off your face.

check.q: Why should you never use a wet towel to pick up a hot pan?
choices: The water turns to steam and burns through to your hand
check.why: Water in the cloth becomes steam against your skin. Use a dry mitt or pot holder.

check.q: Which way should pot handles point on the stove?
choices: Toward the back or side, over the counter
Straight out front for easy grabbing
It does not matter on an electric stove
check.why: Handles turned in cannot be knocked by an elbow or grabbed by a child.

lessons.title: Cuts and Falls
lessons.mainIdea: A sharp knife, a steady board and a dry floor prevent most cuts and falls.
reading: A dull knife slides off a tomato skin and into a finger. A sharp knife bites in where you point it. That is why a *sharp knife* is the safer one: it takes less force, so it does not slip. Keep the board from sliding by laying a damp towel under it. Curl the fingers of your holding hand into a claw so the knuckles, not the fingertips, face the blade.

Cut on a board, never in your hand. Cut away from your body. Never try to catch a falling knife; step back and let it land. Carry a knife at your side, point down, blade toward the back, and tell people "knife behind you" when you pass. Never leave a knife in a sink of soapy water where a hand will find it by accident. Wash it, dry it and put it away.

Other sharp things hide in the kitchen: the lid of an opened can, the blade of a blender or food processor, a box grater, a broken glass. Sweep broken glass with a broom, not your fingers, and wrap it in newspaper before it goes in the trash. Unplug a blender before you reach into it, and wash its blade separately, holding the base.

Falls happen on wet floors and from chairs used as ladders. Wipe up every spill the moment it happens, water or grease, and say "spill" so nobody steps in it. Use a step stool with a handrail to reach a high shelf, not a chair and not the counter. Keep cabinet doors and drawers closed. Tie shoelaces, and wear closed-toe shoes in a lab, because a dropped knife or a splash of oil lands on feet.

words.d: the safer knife: it needs less force, so it does not slip off food and into a hand
curling the fingers of the holding hand so the knuckles guide the blade and fingertips stay back

look.title: Two Minutes in a Busy Kitchen
look.text: A cook drops a knife and grabs for it. Another leaves a paring knife in the dishwater. A third stands on a swivel chair to reach the colander. A puddle of oil from a spilled bottle sits by the stove. Someone reaches into the blender to loosen a stuck strawberry while it is still plugged in.
look.prompt: Rank these from most to least dangerous, and give the safe move for each.

check.q: A knife slips off the counter and falls. What do you do?
choices: Step back and let it fall
check.why: Never catch a falling knife; step back and pick it up once it lands.

check.q: Why is a dull knife more dangerous than a sharp one?
choices: It needs more force and slips off food
check.why: A dull blade requires force and skids off the food; a sharp one cuts where it is aimed.

check.q: You need a bowl from the top shelf. What do you stand on?
choices: A step stool with a handrail
check.why: A step stool is made for climbing; chairs and counters cause falls.

lessons.title: Electric Shock and Cords
lessons.mainIdea: Water and electricity never mix; keep cords dry, short and unplugged before you reach in.
reading: A toaster with a slice stuck in it, and a fork in someone's hand. The metal fork touches the heating element and the current runs up the fork into the person. Always *unplug* an appliance before you reach into it, fix it, or clean it. Then use wooden tongs for the toaster, and let it cool.

Water carries electricity. Never plug in or unplug anything with wet hands, and never use an appliance near a full sink. If a plugged-in appliance falls into water, do not reach for it. Unplug it first, or turn off the circuit breaker if you cannot reach the plug safely. Kitchens have special outlets called *GFCI* outlets, with test and reset buttons, that shut off power in a fraction of a second when they sense a fault. Test them monthly.

Cords cause accidents in two ways. A cord that hangs over the counter edge is a cord a child or a dog can pull, bringing a kettle of boiling water down with it. A cord that lies across a hot burner melts, and a melted cord can shock or start a fire. Route cords along the back of the counter. Pull plugs out by the plug, not by the cord, so the wires inside stay attached.

Look at cords before you use them. Frayed insulation, exposed wire, a plug that is warm or scorched, or an appliance that buzzes, smells hot or sparks all mean stop, unplug and tell an adult. Do not overload one outlet with a power strip full of high-heat appliances; a toaster oven, a kettle and a microwave together can trip a breaker or heat the wiring.

words.d: to disconnect an appliance from the outlet; do it before reaching inside or cleaning it
a ground-fault outlet with test and reset buttons that cuts power fast when it senses a fault; required near water
the switch in the electrical panel that shuts off power to part of the house

look.title: The Toast Is Stuck
look.text: A slice of bread is jammed in the toaster and it is still plugged in and warm. On the counter beside it are a metal fork, a pair of wooden tongs, and a glass of water. The cord runs across the front of the counter and dangles near the floor.
look.prompt: Write the steps to get the toast out safely, in order, and then fix what is wrong with the cord.

check.q: Toast is stuck in the toaster. What is the first step?
choices: Poke it out with a fork
check.why: Unplug before reaching into any appliance; metal in a live toaster can shock you.

check.q: A plugged-in hand mixer falls into a sink of water. What do you do?
choices: Grab it fast before it shorts out
Unplug it or shut off the breaker before touching it
Lift it out with a towel
check.why: Water carries current. Cut the power first, then retrieve the appliance.

check.q: What does a GFCI outlet do?
choices: Cuts power in a fraction of a second when it senses a fault
Stops the toaster from burning bread
check.why: GFCI outlets protect against shock near water by shutting off power almost instantly.

lessons.title: The Grease Fire
lessons.mainIdea: For a grease fire: turn off the heat, slide a lid over the pan, and never use water.
reading: Oil in a pan can get hot enough to light itself. When it does, you have seconds, and the first move is the burner: turn it *off*. The second move is to cut off the air. Take a metal lid or a baking sheet, hold it with a mitt, and slide it over the pan from the near edge, keeping your arm out from over the flames. No air, no fire. Leave the lid on until the pan is completely cool.

If there is no lid, pour *baking soda* on a small fire. A lot of it, not a pinch. Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when heated, which smothers the flames. Salt also works by smothering. Never use flour, sugar or baking mix; fine powders can ignite in the air and turn a small fire into a fireball.

Never, ever use *water*. Water is heavier than oil, so it sinks under the burning grease, boils instantly and blasts flaming oil out of the pan and across the kitchen. Do not carry the burning pan to the sink or outside either; the flames blow back on you and the oil sloshes. The pan stays where it is.

If the lid and the baking soda do not work, or if the fire has spread past the pan to a cabinet or a curtain, it is no longer a pan fire. Get everyone out, close the door behind you and call 911 from outside. A kitchen fire extinguisher is for a fire still small enough to face; the next lesson shows how to use one. Prevention is easier: never leave hot oil unattended, heat oil on medium, and keep a lid within reach every time you fry.

words.d: a fire in cooking oil or fat; smother it with a lid or baking soda, never water
sodium bicarbonate; releases carbon dioxide when heated and can smother a small grease fire
to put out a fire by cutting off its air

look.title: Order the Grease-Fire Steps
look.text: Here are six actions in scrambled order: slide a lid over the pan; turn off the burner; call 911 from outside if it spreads; pour a cup of water on it; leave the lid on until the pan is cool; carry the pan to the sink. Two of them are things you must never do.
look.prompt: Write the correct steps in order, cross out the two forbidden ones, and explain what each forbidden one would cause.

check.q: Oil in a skillet catches fire. What is the first step?
choices: Carry the pan to the sink
check.why: Cut the heat first, then smother the flames with a lid.

check.q: Why does water make a grease fire worse?
choices: It cools the oil too fast
It sinks under the oil, boils and throws burning grease into the air
It puts out the pilot light
check.why: Water is heavier than oil; it flashes to steam under the grease and sprays flaming oil out of the pan.

check.q: Which powder can smother a small grease fire?
check.why: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide and smothers flames. Flour and sugar can ignite.

lessons.title: PASS and the Extinguisher
lessons.mainIdea: Use a fire extinguisher with PASS: pull, aim at the base, squeeze, sweep, with your back to the exit.
reading: Find the *fire extinguisher* in your kitchen or lab right now, before you need it. It should be near an exit, not behind the stove where the fire would be. Read the label: a home kitchen extinguisher is usually rated ABC, meaning it works on ordinary materials (A), flammable liquids like grease (B) and electrical fires (C). Restaurant kitchens use a Class K extinguisher made for deep fryers.

The steps spell *PASS*. Pull the pin at the top of the handle. Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire, not the flames, because the fuel is at the bottom. Squeeze the handle. Sweep the nozzle side to side across the base until the fire is out. Stand about six to eight feet back to start and move closer as the fire dies down.

Before you use it, make two decisions. Is the fire small, meaning no bigger than a wastebasket, and not spreading? And is the exit behind you, so you can back out if it grows? If either answer is no, do not fight the fire. Leave, close the door, and call 911. An extinguisher empties in seconds; it gets one try.

Afterward, watch the spot for a few minutes in case it lights again, and open windows to clear the powder. Even a partly used extinguisher must be replaced or recharged. Check the gauge on any extinguisher once a month: the needle should sit in the green. Install a smoke alarm near the kitchen and test it monthly too; most kitchen fires start on the stove, and most are found early by a working alarm.

words.d: a pressurized canister that sprays a fire-smothering agent; kitchen models are rated ABC or K
pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze the handle, sweep side to side
the bottom of the flames where the fuel is; aiming at the flames themselves does nothing

look.title: Fight or Flee?
look.text: Three scenes. One: a small fire in a toaster, contained, with the door to the hallway right behind you. Two: flames climbing the curtain above the stove and reaching the cabinets, with the only door on the far side of the stove. Three: a trash can fire the size of a basketball in the corner near the exit.
look.prompt: For each scene, say whether you would use the extinguisher or leave and call 911, and name the two questions that decide it.

check.q: What does the A in PASS stand for?
choices: Aim at the base of the fire
check.why: Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire, where the fuel is, not at the flames.

check.q: Where should you stand when using an extinguisher?
choices: Between the fire and the exit, with your back to the exit
In the doorway of another room
check.why: Keep the exit behind you so you can back out if the fire grows.

check.q: Flames have spread from the pan to the cabinets above the stove. What do you do?
choices: Use the extinguisher from up close
Get out, close the door and call 911
check.why: A spreading fire is too big for an extinguisher; leave, close the door and call 911.

lessons.title: Oven, Range and Appliances
lessons.mainIdea: Never leave the stove unattended, keep the area clear, and know how to shut off every appliance.
reading: The most common cause of kitchen fires is a stove left alone. Oil heats faster than people expect, a towel slides onto a burner, a pot boils dry. The rule is simple: if you are frying, grilling or broiling, stay in the kitchen. If you leave the room, turn the burner off. Set a timer for anything simmering or baking so it cannot be forgotten.

Keep the *cook zone* clear. Nothing that can burn within three feet of the stovetop: no towels, paper, oven mitts, plastic bags, wooden spoons or cereal boxes. Wear short or rolled sleeves. Clean grease off the stovetop and out of the range hood filter, because old grease is fuel. On a gas stove, if you smell gas and the burner did not light, turn the knob off, do not light anything, and open a window.

Ovens have their own rules. Open the door and stand to the side for a second before leaning in. If something catches fire inside the oven, keep the door closed and turn the oven off; the fire will smother itself. The same goes for a fire inside a microwave: keep the door shut, turn it off, unplug it. Do not put metal in the microwave, and do not run it empty.

Small *appliances* like toaster ovens, air fryers, slow cookers and electric kettles get hot on the outside too. Give them space from the wall and from each other, unplug them when they are not in use, and never wrap the cord around a hot unit. Know where the stove knobs are without looking, and where the breaker panel is. In an emergency, you shut things off by feel and by memory, not by reading.

words.d: left with nobody watching; an unattended stove is the top cause of kitchen fires
the area within three feet of the stovetop, kept clear of anything that can burn
the vent above the stove; its filter collects grease that must be cleaned out

look.title: A Fire in the Oven
look.text: A cheese-topped casserole bubbles over, and the drips on the oven floor catch fire. Through the oven window you can see flames. Your first instinct is to open the door and grab the dish.
look.prompt: Explain why opening the door is the wrong move and write the three things you would do instead.

check.q: What is the most common cause of kitchen fires?
check.why: Most kitchen fires begin on a stove nobody is watching.

check.q: Something catches fire inside the oven. What should you do?
choices: Open the door and pull it out
Keep the door closed and turn the oven off
Fan the oven with a towel
check.why: A closed oven starves the fire of air; opening the door feeds it oxygen.

check.q: A gas burner clicks but does not light and you smell gas. What is right?
choices: Turn the knob off and open a window
check.why: Turn off the gas, do not light anything, and let fresh air clear the room.

lessons.title: Treating a Cut
lessons.mainIdea: For a cut: wash your hands, press with a clean cloth, rinse, bandage, and get help if it will not stop bleeding.
reading: The knife slips and there is blood on the board. First, stop and put the knife down. Wash your hands if you can, then press a clean cloth or paper towel firmly on the cut. Steady *pressure* is what stops bleeding. Hold it, do not peek every few seconds, and raise the hand above the heart if you can. Most small cuts stop within a few minutes.

Once the bleeding slows, rinse the cut under clean running water to wash out anything in it. Do not use hydrogen peroxide or alcohol inside the wound; they damage the tissue. Pat it dry with a clean cloth, apply a thin layer of antibiotic ointment if you have it, and cover it with a clean *bandage*. In a food lab, cover the bandage with a disposable glove before touching food again.

Some cuts need a doctor. Get help if the bleeding does not stop after steady pressure, if the cut is deep or gaping, if it is on the face or over a joint, if something is stuck in it, or if it came from a dirty or rusty object. Bleeding that spurts or soaks through a cloth is an emergency; call 911 and keep pressing.

The food on the board is done. Anything the blood touched goes in the trash, and the board, the knife and the counter get washed and sanitized before work continues. Tell the teacher or an adult about every cut, even a small one. Write it down if the lab keeps an injury log; the point is not blame but finding the pattern that caused it.

words.d: pressing firmly on a wound with a clean cloth to stop bleeding; the first step for any cut
a clean covering that protects a wound; in a kitchen, cover it with a glove before touching food

look.title: The Slip on the Onion
look.text: A student cuts the side of a finger while slicing an onion. The cut bleeds steadily but does not spurt. The student's first move is to hold it under the faucet, and then to pour hydrogen peroxide on it from the first aid kit.
look.prompt: Rewrite what the student did into the correct order of steps, and say which of the two moves was a mistake and why.

check.q: What is the first thing to do for a bleeding cut?
choices: Press a clean cloth firmly on it
Run cold water on it for ten minutes
Wrap it in a rubber band
check.why: Firm, steady pressure with a clean cloth stops bleeding.

check.q: When does a cut need emergency help?
choices: When it is on a finger
When it will not stop bleeding or is spurting
When it happened on a cutting board
check.why: Bleeding that spurts or does not stop with pressure is an emergency; call 911.

check.q: You have bandaged a cut and want to keep cooking. What goes over the bandage?
check.why: A glove over the bandage keeps blood and bandage out of the food.

lessons.title: Treating a Burn
lessons.mainIdea: Cool a burn under cool running water, cover it loosely, and never put ice, butter or ointment on it.
reading: A hand brushes the oven rack. The skin turns red and starts to sting. Get it under *cool running water* right away, from the tap, not ice cold, and keep it there for at least ten minutes if you can. Cooling stops the heat from going deeper into the skin. Take off rings or watches near the burn before it swells.

Do not use ice; it damages burned skin further. Do not put on butter, oil, toothpaste or grease, which trap the heat in and can cause infection. After cooling, cover the burn loosely with a clean, dry cloth or a sterile non-stick dressing. Do not pop a *blister*; the skin over it protects the raw layer underneath.

Burns are graded by depth. A first-degree burn is red and painful, like a mild sunburn. A second-degree burn blisters. A third-degree burn looks white, leathery or charred and may not hurt at all because the nerves are damaged. Any burn larger than the palm of your hand, any burn on the face, hands, feet or a joint, and any third-degree burn needs a doctor, and a large or deep burn means 911.

For a scald from hot liquid soaked into clothing, get the clothing off fast unless it is stuck to the skin; the wet cloth keeps burning. For a grease splash, same rule: cool water, then cover. Report every burn to the teacher. Then look at what caused it, because the fix for a burn is almost always something you can change next time: a mitt, a handle turned in, a lid tilted the other way.

words.d: the first treatment for a burn: tap water, not ice, run over the burn for at least ten minutes
a fluid-filled bubble over a burn; leave it unbroken because it protects the skin beneath
a burn through all layers of skin, white or charred and often painless; always an emergency

look.title: Burn Depths and What They Look Like
rows: first-degree: red, painful, no blister (layers of skin affected)
third-degree: white or charred, may be painless (layers, all the way through)
minutes under cool running water, at least
look.prompt: A burn from a steam scald has blistered. What degree is it, and what do you do and not do about the blister?

check.q: What is the first treatment for a burn?
check.why: Cool tap water for at least ten minutes stops the heat from going deeper. Ice damages the skin.

check.q: A burn has formed a blister. What do you do with it?
choices: Pop it with a clean pin
Leave it alone and cover loosely
check.why: The blister protects the raw skin under it; leave it intact.

check.q: A burn looks white and leathery and does not hurt. What does that mean?
choices: It is a third-degree burn and needs emergency care
check.why: No pain with white or charred skin means the nerves are damaged; that is a third-degree burn.

lessons.title: When to Call 911
lessons.mainIdea: Call 911 for fire, trouble breathing, heavy bleeding, a large burn, or anyone unconscious; know the address before you dial.
reading: The hardest part of an emergency is deciding it is one. Call *911* when a fire is not out after the lid, when someone cannot breathe or is choking and cannot cough, when bleeding spurts or soaks through cloth, when a burn is large or deep, when someone is unconscious, or when someone has swallowed a chemical. If you are not sure, call. The dispatcher would rather answer a call that was not needed than miss one that was.

Know your *address* before the emergency. In a school lab that means the school name, the street, and the room number. On the phone, say where you are first, then what happened. Stay on the line; the dispatcher will tell you what to do while help is coming. Speak slowly. Send someone to the door to wave the ambulance in.

For choking, the sign is a person who cannot speak, cough or breathe and may grab their throat. If they can cough, let them cough. If they cannot, call 911 and, if you are trained, give back blows and abdominal thrusts. First-aid training from the Red Cross or a similar group teaches this and CPR in one afternoon, and every kitchen worker should have it.

Keep a list where everyone can see it: 911, the Poison Control number, the school office or a parent's number, and the address. Keep the first aid kit stocked and in a marked spot. Practice matters. A class that has walked through "what would we do if" acts in seconds, and seconds are what a kitchen emergency gives you.

words.d: the emergency number in the United States for fire, police and ambulance
the exact location you give the dispatcher first: building, street and room
the person who answers 911, sends help and gives instructions while it comes

look.title: Call or Handle It?
look.text: Five moments: a paper cut on a thumb; a classmate who has gone quiet and is grabbing his throat after a bite of hot dog; a grease fire that went out under the lid; a burn the size of a quarter on a forearm; a student who fainted and is not waking up.
look.prompt: Sort them into call 911 now, handle with first aid, and handle then tell an adult. Say what you would tell the dispatcher for the 911 ones.

check.q: Which situation means call 911 right away?
choices: A person who is choking and cannot cough or speak
A small cut that stopped bleeding
A grease fire that went out under the lid
A first-degree burn on a fingertip
check.why: Someone who cannot breathe, cough or speak needs emergency help immediately.

check.q: What do you tell the dispatcher first?
check.why: Location comes first so help can be sent even if the call is cut off.

check.q: A classmate is coughing hard after a bite of food went down wrong. What do you do?
choices: Slap her on the back hard
Let her keep coughing and watch closely
check.why: If a person can cough, air is moving; let them cough and act only if they cannot.

lessons.title: The Major Allergens
lessons.mainIdea: Nine foods cause most serious allergic reactions, and even a trace can be dangerous to someone allergic.
reading: A friend at your table takes a bite of a cookie and, within minutes, her lips swell and her breathing sounds tight. That is a *food allergy*: the body's defense system treats a harmless food as an attacker. Reactions range from hives and an itchy mouth to *anaphylaxis*, a whole-body reaction that closes the airway and drops blood pressure. Anaphylaxis can kill within minutes.

In the United States, nine foods are the *major allergens* named by law: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish such as shrimp and crab, tree nuts such as almonds and walnuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. Sesame was added to the list in 2023. These nine cause most serious reactions, though a person can be allergic to almost anything.

The amount does not have to be large. For some people, a knife that spread peanut butter and was wiped on a towel carries enough peanut to cause a reaction. That is why allergens are handled like raw chicken: separate tools, separate boards, hands washed with soap and water, and surfaces scrubbed. Hand sanitizer does not remove allergen proteins; soap and water do.

Many people with severe allergies carry an *epinephrine auto-injector*, a pen-shaped device that injects a dose of medicine into the thigh. If someone is having a serious reaction, help them use it, then call 911, because the medicine wears off and a second reaction can follow. Ask about allergies before you cook for anyone, and take the answer seriously. "A little won't hurt" is not true.

words.d: an immune reaction to a food protein; can range from hives to anaphylaxis
a severe, fast, whole-body allergic reaction that can close the airway; call 911
the nine foods named by U.S. law: milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, sesame
a pen-shaped device that injects emergency allergy medicine into the thigh

look.title: The Peanut Butter Knife
look.text: One student spreads peanut butter on crackers, wipes the knife with the shared dish towel, and rinses the knife under water. A second student, who is allergic to peanuts, uses that towel to dry her hands, then uses the same knife to cut an apple.
look.prompt: Trace the peanut protein from the jar to the second student, and name each step where soap, a separate tool or a fresh towel would have stopped it.

check.q: How many major food allergens are named by U.S. law?
check.why: Nine: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame.

check.q: Someone is having anaphylaxis and has an epinephrine auto-injector. What is the order?
choices: Wait to see if it gets worse, then call
Help with the auto-injector, then call 911
Give water and have them lie down
check.why: Epinephrine first, then 911, because the medicine can wear off and the reaction can return.

check.q: Why is hand sanitizer not enough after handling peanuts?
choices: It kills bacteria but does not remove allergen proteins
check.why: Allergen proteins must be washed away with soap and water; sanitizer leaves them on the skin.

lessons.title: Reading the Label for Allergens
lessons.mainIdea: Check the ingredient list and the Contains line every time, because recipes change.
reading: Pick up a package of granola bars and turn it over. Under the *ingredient list* there is often a line in bold: "Contains: milk, peanuts, soy." U.S. law requires packaged foods to name any of the nine major allergens in plain words, either in the ingredient list or in a *Contains statement* right below it. "Whey" must be labeled as milk; "albumin" as egg.

Some labels add a line such as "May contain tree nuts" or "Made in a facility that also processes peanuts." These *advisory statements* are voluntary and mean the food could have picked up traces on shared equipment. For someone with a severe allergy, that is a reason to skip the product. Never assume; a food with no advisory line is not promised to be trace-free.

Read the label every single time, even on a food you have bought a hundred times. Companies change recipes, and the new version can add an allergen without changing the front of the box. Read it at the store, and read it again before you cook. In a lab, keep the packages until the food is served so the label can be checked if someone asks.

Allergens hide in unexpected places. Soy in bread and chocolate, milk in deli meat, egg in some pasta and salad dressings, wheat in soy sauce, fish in Worcestershire sauce, peanuts in some chili and mole sauces. If a dish is for someone with an allergy and you cannot read a label for every ingredient, do not serve it. Say so plainly. A missed meal is nothing compared to a missed allergen.

words.d: the list on a package of everything in the food, in order from most to least
the bold line under the ingredients that names any major allergens in the food
a voluntary warning such as "may contain" that the food could carry traces from shared equipment

look.title: Read This Label
look.text: Ingredients: whole grain oats, sugar, sunflower oil, honey, rice flour, whey, natural flavor, soy lecithin, salt. Contains: milk, soy. May contain peanuts and tree nuts. A classmate with a tree-nut allergy asks if she can have one. Another classmate, allergic to milk, says he does not see "milk" in the ingredients so it must be fine.
look.prompt: Answer both classmates using the label, and explain which word in the ingredient list the second classmate missed.

check.q: Where does U.S. law require major allergens to be named?
choices: Only on the front of the package
In the ingredient list or a Contains statement below it
check.why: Packaged foods must name the nine major allergens in plain words in the ingredients or a Contains line.

check.q: A label says "May contain tree nuts." What does that mean?
choices: Tree nuts are a listed ingredient
The food could carry traces from shared equipment
check.why: An advisory statement warns of possible traces from shared lines; people with severe allergies should avoid it.

check.q: You have bought the same crackers for years. Do you still read the label?
choices: Yes, every time, because recipes change
Only if the box looks different
check.why: Companies change recipes without warning; check the label every purchase and before cooking.

review.q: Which is the correct order for a grease fire?
choices: Carry the pan outside, then call 911
Turn off the burner, slide on a lid, leave it until cool
Open a window, fan the flames, call 911
review.why: Heat off, smother with a lid, leave the lid on. Never water, never move the pan.
Pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze the handle, sweep side to side.

review.q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a dull one?
choices: It needs less force, so it does not slip
review.why: A dull knife needs force and skids off food; a sharp one cuts where it is aimed.

review.q: Toast is stuck in a plugged-in toaster. What is the first step?
review.why: Always unplug before reaching into an appliance.

review.q: A burn on the wrist is red and blistered. What is the first treatment?
choices: Cool running water for at least ten minutes
review.why: Cool tap water stops the heat going deeper; never ice, butter or popping blisters.

review.q: Which of these is a major food allergen under U.S. law?
review.why: Sesame joined milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat and soy as the ninth major allergen.

review.q: A classmate is silent, grabbing his throat and cannot cough. What is right?
choices: Call 911 and give back blows and abdominal thrusts if trained
review.why: No cough, no speech and no breath means a blocked airway; act and call 911.

review.q: Fire is inside the oven. What should you do?
choices: Keep the door closed and turn the oven off
Open the door and pull out the dish
Pour baking soda through the door
Spray it with the sink hose
review.why: A closed oven starves the fire of air; opening the door feeds it.
